Pregnancy

Psoriasis in pregnancy: planning treatment that fits

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Psoriasis does not rule out pregnancy or a healthy baby. Some people find their skin improves while pregnant; others notice little change or a flare. The most useful preparation is a treatment review with your dermatologist and maternity team, ideally before conception. The aim is to control the condition with an appropriate plan rather than assume that all treatment must stop.

What pregnancy can change

Symptoms may improve, remain stable or become worse during pregnancy. It is not possible to predict your experience from someone else’s, and improvement during one pregnancy does not guarantee the same pattern next time.

Flares after birth are common, so discuss postpartum care before the baby arrives. There is no fixed six-week deadline and no promise that the flare will be milder than your earlier disease.

Tell the team about painful or swollen joints as well as skin symptoms. Psoriatic arthritis, sleep disruption and the effect on everyday life can influence treatment choices.

Keep the risk discussion individual

Research on fertility and pregnancy outcomes is mixed. Severe disease, associated health conditions and medicines may all contribute to findings, making it difficult to attribute a risk to psoriasis alone.

Some studies report higher rates of complications such as preterm birth or pre-eclampsia, while others do not. These associations do not predict what will happen in an individual pregnancy. A psoriasis diagnosis is not evidence that your baby will have a birth defect.

Your maternity team can review blood pressure, general health, disease activity and whether additional monitoring is appropriate. Medication review is important, but untreated illness and the impact of painful skin also deserve attention.

Low birth weight is another outcome reported in some studies of more severe psoriasis. Differences in smoking, body weight, other illnesses and treatment can affect these findings; mild disease should not be assigned zero risk and severe disease does not mean a poor outcome is inevitable.

Start with a complete medicine review

Bring a list of prescribed creams, tablets, injections, supplements and non-prescription products. Include the actual names rather than only saying that you use a steroid or an immune medicine.

Some treatments can continue, some need changing and some require a waiting period before conception. Ask for the contraception and timing advice in writing. Do not use a single waiting period for every medicine.

If pregnancy occurs unexpectedly, contact the prescriber promptly. If you are taking methotrexate for psoriasis or acitretin, seek advice immediately before another dose. An exposure needs individual assessment; it is not proof that a baby has been harmed.

Do not abruptly abandon every other treatment because you have a positive test. The team can help you avoid both harmful exposure and an unnecessary severe flare.

If a pregnancy-exposure registry is available for your medicine, the care team may offer information about voluntary participation. This gathers safety information and does not replace your clinical care.

Options that may be considered during pregnancy

Bland emollients can help dryness and are often part of routine care. A prescribed topical corticosteroid may also be used, with the strength, amount, body site and duration chosen carefully. Skin treatment is not automatically risk-free simply because it is a cream.

For more extensive disease, narrowband UVB phototherapy may be an option under medical supervision. Ask about folic acid during treatment. A tanning bed is not a substitute for a controlled phototherapy course.

PUVA combines a light-sensitising medicine with UVA and is generally avoided during pregnancy. It is a different treatment from narrowband UVB.

When topical treatment and light therapy are insufficient, specialists may consider a systemic medicine. Some biologics have substantially more pregnancy data than others. Certolizumab, for example, crosses the placenta only minimally and can be used when clinically appropriate.

Do not assume all biologic injections share the same advice. The choice and timing depend on the particular medicine, disease control and pregnancy circumstances. Make sure the baby’s clinician knows about pregnancy exposure so any advice about live vaccines is specific to that medicine and the local schedule.

Medicines needing particular caution

Methotrexate should not be used to treat psoriasis during pregnancy. Conception planning requires a prescribed stopping and replacement plan; recommendations and product labels differ on the waiting interval.

Acitretin is a retinoid that can cause serious birth defects. Pregnancy must be avoided during treatment and for at least three years after stopping, under the relevant pregnancy-prevention programme. A two-year interval is not adequate current advice.

Topical retinoids such as tazarotene are also avoided in pregnancy. Other products, including certain newer systemic medicines, have insufficient safety information or specific restrictions and need a separate review.

A partner’s use of methotrexate is a different exposure from taking it while pregnant. Available paternal data are reassuring, although manufacturer precautions may advise waiting. The partner should discuss the applicable guidance rather than stop a successful treatment without advice.

Make a plan for feeding and the weeks after birth

Psoriasis itself does not prevent breastfeeding. A medicine’s advice during pregnancy does not automatically tell you whether it is suitable while breastfeeding, so review the postpartum prescription separately.

Some biologics can be compatible with breastfeeding; others have less evidence or require a different plan. There is no blanket need to avoid all biologic treatment until weaning.

If treatment is needed on the nipple or areola, the prescriber should choose an appropriate product and explain timing and removal before feeding. Prevent direct contact between the baby and treated skin. Tell the team if cracks, pain or a flare interfere with feeding.

Arrange access to a prescription review before symptoms become difficult to manage. Seek urgent care for a widespread pustular rash with fever or feeling very unwell during pregnancy; that pattern needs assessment rather than routine home care.

Oral retinoids are generally avoided while breastfeeding. Methotrexate and other systemic medicines need indication- and dose-specific specialist advice; do not assume that a drug’s pregnancy rule settles its lactation use. Dithranol can irritate skin and should not be treated as an automatic breastfeeding alternative, especially near areas the baby touches.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

MotherToBaby describes variable psoriasis course and mixed observational pregnancy-outcome evidence, supporting individual planning rather than blanket reassurance or stopping all treatment.

Pregnancy-prevention guidance for acitretin requires at least three years after stopping. Methotrexate and each biologic need their own preconception, pregnancy and breastfeeding plan.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you prepare a medicine list and questions for the dermatology and maternity teams, including a plan for postpartum flares and feeding.

When to seek help

Contact the prescriber immediately after pregnancy exposure to methotrexate or acitretin and before another dose. A widespread pustular rash with fever or severe illness needs urgent care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Symptoms can change during pregnancy and commonly flare after birth.
  • Review every treatment before conception where possible.
  • Acitretin requires at least three years of pregnancy avoidance after stopping.
  • Biologic and breastfeeding advice must be specific to the medicine.

Frequently asked questions

Must I stop every psoriasis medicine to become pregnant?

No. Some treatments are suitable and others need changing or a waiting period. Make a plan with the prescriber before trying to conceive.

Will pregnancy clear my skin?

It may improve, but it can also remain unchanged or worsen. Keep a plan for pregnancy and postpartum symptoms.

Does a biologic injection mean I cannot breastfeed?

Not automatically. Compatibility depends on the specific medicine and your baby’s circumstances; several have reassuring lactation evidence.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
